title: Shape when knitting in pattern with Cut 'n Sew
metaTitle: Cut and Sew Necklines on a Knitting Machine (Clean Finish)
metaDescription: Learn how to cut and sew your knitted fabric for clean, professional necklines. A simple solution when shaping isn’t enough.
question: How do I shape a neckline without losing my lace or tuck pattern?
hook: Stop fighting with complex stitches and start shaping like a pro.
bubbleAnswer: Forget hand-manipulation. Use Cut 'n Sew to secure your knitting with a sewing machine and cut the shape you need.
mediaAlt: Sue demonstrating how to secure a knitted curve with a sewing machine before cutting.
bridge: Shaping while knitting complex patterns like lace or Fair Isle is a recipe for dropped stitches and frustration. The Cut 'n Sew method lets you knit 'yardage' first, focusing entirely on your stitch pattern. Then, you use a sewing machine to secure the stitches and cut the exact shape you need. It’s the ultimate shortcut for perfect necklines and armholes.

quickAction: Use an unneeded swatch and draw a curve on it with a pen
If desired, mark a neckline shape. Use a KIN neckline template to guide your shaping →
Sew along the marked line with a sewing machine or serger
Take a deep breath and cut 1/4–3/8 inch from the stitching line with a sharp pair of scissors
Observe the stability of the cut edge

title: The Perfect Sandwich Band
metaTitle: Create a Professional Neckline Finish on Your Knitting Machine
metaDescription: Learn how to hide raw edges with a clean, reversible band finish. This simple technique gives your knitted necklines a polished, boutique-quality result.
question: How do I create a clean, professional band finish for my neckline?
hook: Give your necklines a boutique-quality finish that looks great on both sides.
bubbleAnswer: Encase the raw edge between two knitted layers for a clean, reversible finish - perfect for cut 'n sew.
mediaAlt: Sue demonstrating how to sandwich a cut knitted edge between two band layers on the machine.
bridge:
This sandwich band finish (also known as an industrial band) creates a clean, professional edge by enclosing the stitches between two knitted layers. The result is smooth, polished, and looks beautiful on both sides.
It works whether you’re finishing a cut edge or a shaped edge - the goal is the same: completely hide the edge for a refined, finished look.
The secret to a professional result is graded tension - knitting the band slightly tighter at curves so it hugs the neckline without ruffling or flipping.

quickAction: Knit the first half of the band
Hang the neckline edge onto the needles
Knit the second half of the band
Join the bands to enclose the edge

title: Working Within Your Knitting Machine’s Limits
metaTitle: Not Enough Needles on your knitting machine? How to make it work
metaDescription: Struggling with limited needles on your machine? Learn how to adjust yarn, stitch patterns, and construction to knit any size successfully.
question: I don’t have enough needles for this - now what?
bubbleAnswer: Adjust your yarn, stitch pattern, or construction method to create the required width without needing more needles
hook: You can still knit the project you want - even with fewer needles.
bridge: Your machine width is fixed by needle count, but knitting width changes with gauge, yarn, and stitch pattern. Use the Maximum Knitted Width tool to see how wide you can knit with your gauge on your machine.

quickAction: check your gauge Maximum Knitted Width tool
Try a different yarn or stitch pattern
Consider knitting panels
Not sure how to divide your pieces? Use a worksheet to plan sweater panels and keep everything aligned.
👉 Download the Sweaters Panel Planning Worksheet

trySteps: Quick Action Steps
Check your gauge and calculate the maximum width your machine can knit
Try a different yarn that gives fewer stitches per inch for more width
Use a wider stitch pattern like tuck or lace to increase fabric width
Split large pieces into multiple sections and seam them together
Add seams creatively (center, sides, or underarms) to maintain shaping
Consider sideways knitting for larger sizes without adding seams

title: Measure Gauge on a Knitting Machine
metaTitle: How to knit a swatch on the knitting machine
metaDescription: A simple,  accurate way to measure gauge on your knitting machine using stitch and row counts
question: How do I knit a swatch that gives me accurate gauge?
bubbleAnswer: Knit a swatch large enough to measure accurately, work in your intended stitch pattern, and avoid measuring the edges. Mark a section in the center with a set number of stitches and rows so you can measure your fabric without distortion.
hook: Don't count - measure a defined section of stitches and rows.
mediaAlt: accurately measure a gauge swatch for machine knitting
bridge:
Most knitters are taught:
“Measure 4 inches and count stitches”
That works for hand knitting…

But for machine knitting, it can be less reliable.
This method works better because:
  • You don't have to count or guess
  • You’re working with exact stitch counts (like your machine does)
  • You’re not trying to “fit” your knitting into a fixed space
  • You can even account for 1/2 stitch

quickAction: Think in stitches and rows—not inches
Start with a set number of stitches and rows (see guide below)
Measure the space they create
👉 Use the Knit it Now Gauge Calculator to turn your measurements into usable numbers
Calculation Tip: (Number of stitches / width in inches) = Stitches per inch.
Use this gauge—it reflects how your yarn, tension, and machine actually knit.
tryThis.quickActionNote:
MEASURE this many stitches and rows:
Standard (4.5mm)40 stitches × 60 rows
Mid-gauge (6.5mm)30 stitches × 40 rows
Bulky (9mm)20 stitches × 30 rows
These are the stitches and rows to measure - make the swatch larger so you can measure in the center not the edges

title: Joining Fair Isle Panels Without an Ugly Seam
metaDescription: how to seam machine knit fairisle panels
question: How do I join Fair Isle panels without an ugly seam?
bubbleAnswer: Turn the seam into a design feature — don’t try to hide it.
hook: Take a closer look… your seam might be the best part of your Fair Isle panels.
bridge:
Fair Isle panels can create bulky or messy seams if you try to match them perfectly.
Instead of fighting it, treat the seam as a design element — something that adds structure and interest.
A visible join can look intentional and clean, especially with colorwork.

Instead, treat the seam as part of the design:

-add texture
-add contrast
-add structure

Now your seam isn’t something to fix - it’s something to show off.

quickAction: Knit a long I-cord first
Keep your tension consistent (this really matters!)
Hang one panel (right/public side facing you)
Hang the I-cord
Hang the second panel (wrong/private side facing you)
Knit across to join
Bind off
tryThis.quickActionNote: 👉 Result: A raised, polished seam that looks intentional and decorative

title: Changing Colors on the LK150
metaTitle: How to change colors on the LK150
metaDescription: Learn how to change yarn colors on the LK150 without dropping your knitting from the machine.
question: How do I change colors on my LK150?
bubbleAnswer: Color changes don’t have to stop your knitting - once you know this, everything flows.
hook: Changing colors on the LK150 is easier than you might think.
bridge:
Changing colors on the LK150 is simple once you know what to do. The goal is to switch yarns smoothly, make sure the new yarn is feeding correctly, and keep knitting without overthinking the process.

Don’t worry about the yarn tails right now. For this first step, just focus on changing the yarn and keeping your stitches safely on the machine.
memberText: Now that you can change colors, learn how to secure your yarn tails as you knit, make simple stripes, and try single-row stripes with free pass.

quickAction: Remove the working yarn from the yarn feeder
If you aren’t cutting the yarn, loop it around the needle bed or use the <GlossaryTooltip term="yarn-rest">yarn rest</GlossaryTooltip> if yours is in place
Place the new yarn into the yarn feeder, holding it from above and below
Wiggle and pull the yarn gently to make sure it is seated securely
Pull the yarn up and down to make sure it is not caught and feeds smoothly
Secure the tail with a chip clip, clothespin, or hold it with your left hand
Keep knitting
tryThis.quickActionNote: 👉 Don’t worry about finishing the tails yet. You can secure them as you go in the next step.

title: Easy, beautiful texture with tuck stitch
metaTitle: How to Knit Tuck Stitch on the LK150 Knitting Machine
metaDescription: Learn how to knit tuck stitch on the LK150 using manual needle selection and Russell levers to create texture.
question: How do I knit tuck stitch on myLK150?
bubbleAnswer: Use Russell levers and manual needle selection to hold stitches, build loops, and knit them off to create tuck texture
hook: This is a simple technique that opens up a lot of texture options
mediaAlt: Tuck stitch pull up technique on the LK150 knitting machine
bridge: Tuck stitch on the LK150 is created by holding selected needles while the yarn floats across them. After a few passes, those loops are knit off to create texture. Since the LK150 has no punchcards or electronics, you control the stitch pattern entirely by which needles you select and how you use the Russell levers.

quickAction: Cast on 20 stitches and knit a few rows
Use every-other needle selection for a basic tuck pattern
Set Russell levers to II to hold stitches
Knit two passes to build loops
Return levers to I to knit off the loops
Switch needle selection and repeat

trySteps: Step-by-Step Tuck on the LK150
Cast on 20 stitches and knit a few rows
End with the carriage on the right
Move needles 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19 to D position
Set both Russell levers to II
Knit across to the left, then back to the right
Notice loops building over the held needles
Return both Russell levers to I
Knit across to release the loops
Knit back to the right
Move needles 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, and 18 to D position
Set both Russell levers to II
Knit across to the left, then back to the right
Return both Russell levers to I
Knit across to release the loops
Repeat the sequence 5–6 times
Knit a few rows and bind off
Turn your swatch and choose which side you like best
